question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic produce transformation in the person, and if so does it change the person's condition, their orientation to their condition, or both? Record none if no transformation is shown.

sample.text: **[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic produces transformation of both condition and orientation. Hos 9:10 (vc=1632 — VCG-04): "they became detestable like the thing they loved" — condition is transformed: the person's own inner character-quality shifts toward the image of what they worship. Eze 11:21 (vc=1631/65982 — VCG-05): "heart goes after their detestable things" — orientation is transformed: the heart's directional faculty is re-oriented toward idols. The progressive deepening evidence (Eze 8:13; 8:15 — VCG-05: "still greater abominations") shows both condition (progressively more corrupted) and orientation (progressively more firmly directed toward idols) transforming together over time. The Ezekiel restoration (Eze 37:23 — VCG-05) also documents transformation of both condition ("I will save them and cleanse them") and orientation ("they shall not defile themselves anymore with their idols").

Primarily orientation change, with somatic consequence. The M39-B evidence does not name a radical condition-change equivalent to Eph 2:8. 1Ki 8:18 (goodness in the heart) — the inner moral quality shapes the person's orientation toward their actions and toward God. Psa 119:71 ("it is good for me that I was afflicted") — the goodness-evaluation characteristic transforms orientation to affliction (what was suffering becomes recognised as formative). Pro 17:22 — the somatic consequence (healed/dried bones) is a physical condition change produced by the inner orientation change.

Yes — emphatically. 1Cor 15:10: "by the grace of God I am what I am" — identity-constituting transformation. Eph 2:1-5 (SD008): from dead to alive — the most radical condition-change in the corpus. 2Cor 12:9: not condition-change (weakness remains) but orientation-change (weakness-as-theatre-of-grace rather than weakness-as-problem). Both condition-change and orientation-change are evidenced.

*Consistent with prior analysis (SD008, SD032). Adds T5 framing: both types present — unusually complete.*

**[CHAR-21]** E — Both. (1) *Negative condition change*: Jer 2:21 — "turned degenerate and become a wild vine" — the transformation of what was good into what is corrupt; 1Ti 6:5 — "depraved in mind and deprived of the truth" — a constitutional condition-change of the mind; (2) *Negative orientation change*: Jer 3:21 — "perverted their way; forgotten the Lord their God" — the directional orientation of life is twisted from God-toward to God-forgetting; (3) *Positive transformation through remedy*: Eph 4:22-24 — "put off... old self... put on the new self" — the transformation from the corrupt old self to the new-self condition; 2Pe 1:4 — "escaped from the corruption... partakers of the divine nature" — the escape-and-participation transformation.

Ya.ash's sustained operation produces transformation of the person's moral orientation — Jer 2:25 shows a person whose sustained despair-posture has formed them as one who has closed off return. The transformation is of the person's openness to repentance.

question_text: Is the transformation reversible or irreversible in the evidence?

sample.text: The eschatological permanence of de.ra.on (Dan 12:2, Isa 66:24) implies irreversibility at the final horizon. The righteous abhorrence of evil reaches its completion; the condition of being permanently abhorrent cannot be undone.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** The hardening of the heart (Rom 2:5, VSG 3207-001) implies increasing irreversibility in the wickedness-direction: the heart becomes progressively harder, suggesting that the capacity for repentance is not indefinitely available. The eschatological crystallisation in Rev 22:11 ("let the evildoer still do evil... let the righteous still do right") presents the final state as irreversible — moral identity is fixed at the eschatological endpoint.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, in two trajectories. (1) Corrective transformation: where the humiliated person receives the corrective signal, CHAR-2 produces reorientation of inner standing toward proper proportion. (2) Eschatological transformation: 1Cor 15:43 — the body sown in dishonor is raised in glory — the mortal state of humiliation is explicitly transitional rather than final. David's envoys' humiliation is reversible (2Sa 10:5). VCG-04 evidence (Eze 32; Jer 23:40 — perpetual shame) shows humiliation as permanent in judgment contexts. Reversibility depends on whether divine redemption addresses the humiliation.

---

**[CHAR-5]** S — The three-verse corpus does not directly address the reversibility of the transformations produced by semnotēs. The characteristic's relational-ordering effects persist while the characteristic is genuinely present and can be lost if the inner character quality is not maintained.

The evidence distinguishes formal from genuine transformation. The covenant promise (Heb 8:12 — "I will remember their sins no more") names irreversible divine memory-erasure under the new covenant — the propitious act is permanent in its divine dimension. However, the *lo ruchamah* warning (Hos 1:6 — OBS-111-058) shows that mercy can be withdrawn in response to persistent covenant rejection — this is not the reversal of a completed atoning act but the suspension of the mercy relationship before or without that act. The Mat 18:34–35 parable (the unforgiving servant handed over to the jailer) raises questions about the stability of received mercy when inner transformation has not occurred — but this is parabolic and its resolution is not fully settled in the data. OBS-111-035, OBS-111-055, OBS-111-058.

question_text: Does this verse describe a sequence of inner states the characteristic moves the person through — a before, during, and after — and what are those states? Record none if no sequence is shown.

sample.text: **[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. VCG-04 (11 verses) is specifically the conscience-sequence evidence, documenting the characteristic's inner-state progression. The deepening sequence: (1) inner moral knowledge present but conscience beginning to be suppressed — Deu 27:15 (vc=65937 — VCG-04): the person sets up the idol in secret while knowing it is wrong; (2) abomination committed with partial conscience-engagement; (3) full conscience-silencing — Jer 6:15 (vc=1680 — VCG-04); Jer 8:12 (vc=1696 — VCG-04): "not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush"; (4) accumulated weight — Eze 44:13 (vc=66003 — VCG-04): abominations as permanent burden; (5) eschatological exclusion — Rev 21:27 (vc=22 — VCG-05). The restoration sequence (Ezekiel): (1) divine action restores memory — Eze 36:31 (vc=1681); (2) self-loathing emerges; (3) repentance-command — Eze 14:6 (vc=65984); (4) turning from abominations.

Learned contentment is cultivated through lived experience across varying circumstances (Phil 4:11-12) and through the ongoing relationship with God that provides the inner resource (Phil 4:13 — "through him who strengthens me"). The cultivation of M46-D's postures requires both experience and relationship with Christ — neither alone is sufficient.

**[CHAR-15]** E — Yes — a trajectory across the corpus. (1) *Active sinning phase*: Psa 78:17 — "sinned still more... rebelling" — persistent sinning despite divine provision; (2) *Prolonged condition*: Isa 64:5 — "in our sins we have been a long time" — the sinning has become the settled state; (3) *Consequence and doom*: Jer 8:14 — "doomed to perish... poisoned water" — the accumulated sinning produces catastrophic external consequences; (4) *Corporate recognition and confession*: 1Ki 8:47 — "turn their heart... repent and plead... 'We have sinned'" — the consequence drives the recognition; (5) *Divine restoration promise*: Eze 37:23 — cleansed, restored covenant-people identity.

Yes — a simpler sequence: (1) The heart-goodness sequence: good intention in heart (1Ki 8:18) → right action → divine affirmation. (2) The affliction-goodness sequence: affliction → recognised as good (Psa 119:71) → deeper moral formation. (3) The gladness-somatic sequence: glad/good heart (Pro 15:13) → cheerful face → healed bones (Pro 17:22). The sequence in M39-B is shorter and more individual than M39-A's.

Yes — the data contains several explicit and implicit sequences. Q033 answer and OBS-064-029 together establish the most complete account:

**The primary forgiveness sequence (divine forgiveness received):**
- **Before:** Sin committed → guilt accumulated (the debt-state registered by conscience, confirmed by 54 shared verses with R073). The person is in the guilt-state — the legitimate claim stands against them.
- **Access-moment:** Repentance, faith, confession, intercession — the inner orientations through which the person moves toward reception.
- **During:** The divine act of releasing — "your sins are forgiven" (Luk 7:47-48). The moment of pronouncement/act.
- **After (immediate):** Love-orientation produced (Luk 7:47); blessedness named (Rom 4:7); fear/reverence (Psa 130:4). The inner states that follow the forgiveness-event.
- **After (sustained):** Hope (Psa 130:5-7); sustained love-orientation as relational disposition; capacity for horizontal forgiveness (F-003).

**The horizontal forgiveness sequence (human giving):**
- **Before:** Offence received → claim registered (moral awareness of legitimate grievance) → the inner state of withheld grievance (OBS-064-001 — "poisoning of the inner life").
- **Enabling moment:** Compassion (splagchnizomai, Mat 18:27); the heart-level decision to release.
- **During:** The act of forgiving — verbal declaration and/or inner release.
- **After:** Inner freedom from the retained grievance; the relational field reopened (F-008).

question_text: In this verse, by what mechanism does the characteristic produce change — discipline, encounter, gradual formation, sudden transformation, or other? Record none if no mechanism is shown.

sample.text: **[CHAR-2]** E — The deterioration mechanism is progressive self-consolidation through accumulation and spread. 2Ti 3:13 (vc=14451 — VCG-06): "from bad to worse" — each stage of deterioration feeds the next without an external input required. The leaven metaphor (1Cor 5:8 — VCG-05): leaven works by spreading through the whole batch; no additional external leaven is needed — the mechanism is internal propagation through existing constitutional material. Mat 12:45 (vc=65879 — VCG-06): the vacated inner space attracting seven more evil spirits — the mechanism here is vacuum-filling; the absence of positive inner occupation enables the characteristic's deepening. These three mechanisms (progressive self-reinforcement, leaven-spreading, vacuum-filling) are distinct modes of the same self-consolidating dynamic.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Multiple mechanisms are evidenced. *Decisive volitional reorientation:* Act6:7 — priests becoming obedient to the faith as a single decisive act of inner reorientation; Heb11:8 — Abraham obeyed the call as a faith-driven inner response to divine command. *Gradual formation through sustained practice:* Phili2:12 ("always obeyed") — sustained practice without external support forms the dispositional character. *Costly formation through suffering:* Heb5:8 — Christ learning obedience through what he suffered — the mechanism of costly engagement with hardship shapes the disposition at depth. *Spirit-directed sanctification:* 1Pe1:2 — the Spirit's work directs the inner formation toward obedience. *Word-reception:* Rom10:16 and the gospel-obedience cluster — hearing and receiving the gospel as the mechanism of the decisive inner reorientation.

Formation: divine bestowing (VCG02 Spirit-endowment), fear of the LORD (VCG09), hearing and accumulating (VCG03). Deepening: sustained practice in living wisely. Loss: self-attributed wisdom (VCG06) — the person who claims wisdom is closed to receiving it; foolishness as the failure to pursue (Pro 1 inverse).

M01-F's chronic anxiety operates as a sustained **condition** rather than a mechanism producing change. Its resolution (Psa 34:4 anchor: seeking the Lord → deliverance from all fears) uses the mechanism of **divine response to seeking** — not discipline or self-effort but relational engagement with God producing the resolution.

Primarily gradual formation: the virtue-psychology frame (science extract Section 2 — Aristotle via Peterson/Seligman) confirms that the goodness characteristic is formed through habitual practice. Psa 36:3 ("ceased to act wisely and do good") implies the reverse — goodness can be lost through repeated departure. No sudden-transformation mechanism is evidenced in M39-B.

question_text: Does the mechanism differ across contexts in the evidence; if so, how?

sample.text: **[CHAR-19]** E — Yes across VCG registers. (1) *VCG-03 (threshold)*: mechanism is divine patience reaching its limit through counted accumulation (Amos 1:3/6/9); (2) *VCG-02 (revolt)*: mechanism is the degrading systemic effect of persistent inner defiance — Isa 1:5 — continued revolt despite punishment produces whole-person inner deterioration; (3) *VCG-07 (oppressive weight)*: mechanism is the weight-accumulation of individual transgressions binding into a yoke (Lam 1:14) — the additive weight mechanism; (4) *VCG-04 (law-violation)*: mechanism is the legal-standing nullification — Rom 2:25 — "your circumcision becomes uncircumcision" — transgression renders religious identity void by removing its legal validity.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. The judicial mechanism (Rom 1:24, VCG-02) operates at the theological level — God's active response to prior human defection. The gradual-formation mechanism (Eph 4:19 — callousness) operates at the natural-developmental level — the inner person changes through repeated exposure without sudden event. The volitional surrender mechanism (Eph 4:19 — "given themselves up") operates at the level of a decisive inner act. The conscience-defilement mechanism (1Cor 8:7, VCG-03) operates at the level of a specific act against inner conviction. Each mechanism operates in a different contextual register.

**Contrast: B-VCG-01 vs B-VCG-04:** Yes. In the covenant-discipline context (M02-B-VCG-01), the mechanism is external consequence → repentance → relenting of anger. In the righteous-anger context (M02-B-VCG-04), the mechanism is inner perception of injustice → anger → confrontation → reform (Neh 5:6–12 shows the full sequence). The covenant-discipline mechanism is consequence-driven; the righteous-anger mechanism is perception-and-confrontation-driven.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The mechanism of CHAR-6's maintenance is the sustained moral choice to avoid deliberate wrongdoing and to remain in covenant faithfulness to God. Psa 26:6's "I wash my hands in innocence" implies an active, habitual practice. The mechanism of CHAR-6's loss (Hos 8:5) is the sustained choice of idolatry — the repeated moral choices to worship the golden calf rather than God, which over time damage the innocence-capacity until it is no longer accessible.

Yes — the mechanisms are context-differentiated. The encounter mechanism operates in experiential and worship contexts (Psalms — crisis, praise, seeking). The Spirit-infusion mechanism operates in the pneumatological-community context (NT epistolary — Gal, Eph, Rom, Col). The recognition-confrontation mechanism operates in prophetic and apostolic contexts that address moral failure (Eze, Lam, Rom 2). The differentiation is not random — each mechanism is appropriate to its context: the seeking soul receives through encounter; the redeemed community receives through Spirit; the morally blind person is reached through recognition-confrontation. The mechanisms together cover the full range of contexts in which goodness produces transformation. (OBS-067-OBS-025, OBS-067-OBS-035, OBS-067-OBS-039)

question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic operate in relation to suffering or affliction — as a response to it, a product of it, or a context for it? Record none if no such relation is shown.

sample.text: **[CHAR-13]** E — Yes — extensively. The record directly produces physical suffering. Psa 38:3 — "there is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no health in my bones because of my sin" — physical affliction is a direct consequence of the record's weight. Psa 25:18 — "consider my affliction and my trouble, and forgive all my sins" — affliction and sins are placed in parallel as co-present burdens requiring divine attention. Neh 9:37 — "they rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress" — the national sin-record produces the suffering of foreign domination and loss of bodily freedom.

VCG05 (Heb 5:14): the training that forms discernment implies disciplined effort — which can include difficulty. The maturity toward which understanding-training is directed is explicitly eschatologically tested.

**[CLUSTER — T5.4]** E. Suffering is a persistent context across the cluster. The cluster's relationship to suffering is characterised by: (1) righteousness persisting through suffering without being eliminated by it (A2-013); (2) suffering produced by injustice generating the cry for justice (D); (3) the weight of condemnation as a form of suffering resolved by freedom from verdict (E); and (4) the reckoning faculty applied specifically to suffering as its primary object of comparative assessment (F). Righteousness does not remove suffering from the believer's experience — it provides the orientation, resilience, and reckoning capacity needed to traverse it.

M46-A's prophetic judgment passages (Jam 5:1-5; Rev 18:15-19) describe the suffering that comes upon those whose wealth-produced inner closure results in judgment. The merchants weeping (Rev 18:15-19) and the rich howling (Jam 5:1) are the suffering that follows inner-closure's harvest.

question_text: What does the evidence show suffering doing to the characteristic in the person — and record no such effect if none is shown.

sample.text: **[CHAR-4]** E — Suffering *produces and grounds* the characteristic, per Heb5:2. The high priest's being "beset with weakness" — his own experience of creaturely limitation — is the constitutive ground for his capacity for metriopatheō. The suffering/limitation experience is not an obstacle to the characteristic but its enabling condition: genuine acquaintance with one's own weakness produces the empathic basis for measured compassionate dealing with others in their weakness.
No direct evidence of suffering producing understanding in M15-B's VCG corpus.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster reveals two distinct relationships between suffering and the defilement-state. Characteristics 1 and 3 show suffering as revealing or formative. Characteristic 1: the grief at exclusion (Num 9:7) reveals the person's sacral orientation — the grief shows the will directed toward worship rather than away; suffering reveals inner orientation. Characteristic 3: the suffering of exile (Lam 1:17/4:15, Eze 4:13) reveals the defilement publicly — what was hidden in the community's denial (Jer 2:23) becomes undeniable in exile; and the exile-suffering is the context in which memory is activated for repentance (Eze 20:43 — memory in exile leading to self-loathing). Characteristics 2 and 4 show suffering as consequence only. Characteristic 2 is S on suffering-as-producer — the characteristic is generated through desire, habitual sin, and judicial release, not through suffering. Characteristic 4 is S on suffering-as-producer — the characteristic is imposed by an external agent regardless of the person's suffering state. The cluster's differentiated pattern: suffering reveals the defilement-state and activates repentance where the mechanism is covenantal-volitional (Chars 1, 3); suffering is consequence only where the mechanism is internal-moral (Char 2) or externally-imposed (Char 4).

Differentiated by sub-group: M05-B (suffering produces compassion by triggering it); M05-D (suffering tests goodness by revealing whether the commitment persists under cost); M05-E (suffering under provocation tests and reveals gentleness); M05-F (suffering produces the comforter-qualification — 2Cor 1:4 — Group 602: one must have been comforted in one's own affliction to qualify as a genuine comforter of others); M05-G (sharing in suffering deepens the koinōnos bond — 2Cor 1:7 — Group 1057). The common pattern: suffering is not the enemy of the cluster's characteristics but their formation context.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Suffering *reveals* the guilt and *triggers* its recognition. Gen 42:21 — the brothers' current distress reveals their past guilt by creating the interpretive pressure that connects the two; suffering does not produce the guilt (the guilt preceded the suffering) but reveals it by providing the interpretive framework. Ezr 9:7 — captivity, sword, plundering are the outer sufferings that reveal the inner guilt-reality they resulted from; the suffering makes visible what the guilt-state was. Hos 5:15 — "in their distress earnestly seek me" — the distress (which is a form of suffering) is the condition that activates the seeking that follows guilt-acknowledgment.

question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic participate in the longer arc of character formation and sanctification — shaping the person over time — and what does the evidence show of its role in that arc? Record none if no such participation is shown.

sample.text: Participates in negative formation only. Cruelty is the anti-formation condition — the state of the person in whom the governing framework has been removed. No verse shows cruelty contributing to sanctification.

**[C — Justification]** Yes — justification establishes the platform from which sanctification proceeds. "Being justified by his grace we might become heirs" (Tit 3:7) — the becoming of heir-identity is a developmental process. Justification does not complete sanctification — it establishes the conditions under which sanctification can proceed. The cluster shows C as the foundation and A2 (practiced righteousness) as the ongoing formation process built on it.

M46-A's formation trajectory is negative: the prosperity-apostasy pattern represents the formation of closure through unchecked abundance. The at-ease condition (sha.a.nan) is formed over time by sustained material security without spiritual formation countering it.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — as both the negative formation arc's scaling property and the eschatological character-type. (1) *Negative formation*: Luk 16:10 — "dishonest in very little is also dishonest in much" — injustice as a forming character-property that consolidates across all scales; the habituation to small injustices forms the character that then commits large ones; (2) *Emergence within a formed being*: Eze 28:15 — "you were blameless in your ways... till unrighteousness was found in you" — injustice can emerge within an already-formed, previously blameless being; formation does not immunize against the emergence.

question_text: In this verse, is the characteristic oriented toward an eschatological fullness — a future state toward which its present operation points — and what does its present experience anticipate of that fullness? Record none if no such orientation is shown.

sample.text: All seven sub-groups evidence eschatological orientation (see T0.2.3 above for sub-group detail). The cluster's eschatological content varies: love is permanent (M05-A — 1Cor 13:8 — Group 1542); compassion gathers the exiled in a great eschatological restoration (M05-B — Isa 54:7 — Group 1596); mercy is awaited at the last day (M05-C — Jude 21 — Group 1632); goodness moves toward completion and inherits the "good things to come" (M05-D — Heb 10:1 — Group 1099; Phili 1:6 — Group 1098); gentleness inherits the earth and is grounded in the Lord's nearness (M05-E — Mat 5:5 — Group 1261; Phili 4:5 — Group 1103); comfort is eternal (M05-F — 2Th 2:16 — Group 3074; Mat 5:4 — Group 602); fellowship participates in eschatological glory and inheritance (M05-G — 1Pe 5:1 — Group 1057; Act 20:32 — Group 2849). The cluster as a whole is eschatologically constituted — its characteristics are not only present practices but forward-pointing participations in what will be completed and revealed.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment endpoint*: 1Ch 10:13 — "Saul died for his breach of faith" — death as faithlessness's personal eschatological verdict; Dan 9:7 — exile and open shame as the communal eschatological judgment; 2Ch 30:7 — "made them a desolation" — desolation as the nation's judgment; (2) *Restoration endpoint*: Eze 39:26 — "they shall forget their shame and all the treachery they have practiced against me, when they dwell securely in their land with none to make them afraid" — the eschatological fullness is secure dwelling in which the shame of treachery is forgotten; Lev 26:42 — "I will remember my covenant" — covenant-memory restoration as the eschatological goal.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The corpus points contagious sin toward two eschatological trajectories. (1) *Judgment and abandonment*: 1Ki 14:16 — "he will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam" — the ultimate consequence of sustained contagious sin transmission across generations is national abandonment by God; the exile of the Northern Kingdom is the eschatological endpoint of the Jeroboam transmission. (2) *Structural dismantling*: 2Ki 23:15 — Josiah's demolition of the Bethel altar — the physical destruction of the contagious sin's structural legacy points toward the complete eschatological dismantling of all sin-transmitting structures.
